We said what the whole church says. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. The same words the ancient councils hammered out still held among us - true God and true man, one person, two natures. We did not revise Nicaea or Chalcedon. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught his death secures, and where we told someone to look for him now.

God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We held that as a settled ground, not a threat. And we did not send anyone searching their own heart for proof of it. Our own confession says it plainly: Christ himself, not your own conscience, is where election is rightly seen. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

Where we met him present among us now was at the Supper, and here is where our own two cities had to test the question most carefully. We refused two claims. Rome's own mass does not repeat his sacrifice - that was finished once. And his body does not sit locally in the bread the way Wittenberg claimed it did. What we affirmed took both cities and a 1549 agreement to state together: Christ is truly given, by the Spirit's own power, to whoever receives him believing. We tell the sign apart from what it points to, but we never pull them apart. Whether that later word deepens our founder's earlier 'remembrance' reading or only restates it more carefully, we do not claim to know. We hold both as our own.

And we held a believer's life answerable to what was professed. At Geneva, that was the Consistory's own work - pastors and lay elders together, testing whether conduct matched confession. Its harshest tool was exclusion from the Supper itself, and readmission was always held open to genuine repentance. What I cannot give you is what that summons actually felt like to receive, or how an ordinary Sunday service felt to sit through. That texture has not reached us. What we taught, I can show you. What was felt, I cannot.

We will not tell you that the inability itself is a failure, or that managing to believe is the wrong name for what has not yet happened. What we will tell you is where the believing is aimed, and what we held to be given in it, plainly.

Christ is held out in the promise, not discovered by searching inside yourself. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: "We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination." A mind turned only on itself - asking whether it has managed well enough, or believed hard enough - finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward what God has promised in the text, once, rather than toward the self's own performance, endlessly.

What we have of Christ is not a living chain of memory - no one among us met anyone who met him, fifteen hundred years stand between his life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Scripture alone settles what we believe; what it does not yield, we have no standing to require of anyone.

So the honest answer to "I cannot manage to believe" is not that you must manage it better. It is that the promise is not written to be verified by your own certainty about it. It is written to be looked at. Look there - at Christ, held out in the text - not at how convincingly you yourself are looking.

Who is Jesus, how does he stand toward the Father and the Spirit, and what does that make of God? On that question itself, we say what the whole church says - what was settled at Nicaea and Chalcedon, long before our own reforms ever began. One God, three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Son is not made, not a creature, not a lesser divinity placed beneath the Father - he is God himself, eternally begotten, of one substance with the Father. At the incarnation, he took on human nature fully, without confusion and without division, so that the one Christ is both truly God and truly human. All of that we hold without reservation, without addition, and without any claim that it was distinctively ours to settle.

What is distinctly ours - what actually divided us from Rome, and what nearly split the wider Protestant movement at Marburg in 1529 - was never a disagreement about who Christ is in himself. It was what his death secures, how he is given to us at the Supper, and where final authority rests when doctrine is contested. On the first of those: God's own free choice, made before the world existed, determines who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. On the second: Christ is truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing, but his body is not confined to bread that can be broken, chewed, and stored away. On the third: Scripture alone, tested in public argument or built up through sustained teaching, is sufficient to settle what a church must hold - not a council's decree, not an inherited practice simply because it has always been done that way.

So when you ask about the Trinity itself, the answer is: we hold what Nicaea held, what Chalcedon held, what the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed both say plainly. That was never our quarrel, not with Rome and not among ourselves.

God is sovereign - wholly and finally so, over every last thing. That is the first true word. He does not share his rule with anyone, he does not wait on a created will to choose him before deciding whether to save it, and he does not answer to our own sense of what fairness ought to require. Before the world itself began, by his own free choice alone, he decided who would be saved and who would not, and that decision was not made by looking ahead to see what anyone would do or become. Nothing foreseen, nothing earned. Election rests on nothing but God's own will, and that will needs no justification beyond itself.

This is not a threat we hold over anyone. It is the ground we stand on when every other ground gives way. A conscience examined long enough finds no bottom to its own doubt, and a life measured against God's own holiness finds nothing in itself that could possibly be enough. So we do not tell anyone to search inward for proof of election - that road only ends in dread. What we say instead is this: look at Christ, not at yourself. The Second Helvetic Confession says it plainly: Christ is the mirror in which election is rightly seen. The promise is not written to be verified by your own certainty about it. It is written to be looked at, believed, and rested in.

God is also the one who made everything, and he did not step back after making it. His providence is not a distant first cause but continuous, active care over all he made. He governs everything that happens, not as though the world were a mechanism set running and left alone, but as though every moment were still directly in his hand - which it is.

What else is true of him? He is triune - Father, Son, and Spirit, three persons, one God - but that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we say his sovereignty secures: not salvation earned or foreseen, but salvation decided, finished, and held out in the promise to whoever receives Christ believing.

live_attach.answer_text:
Who held the final word over doctrine when we disagreed? The question is sharper than it sounds, because the answer is not the same answer in both our cities.

At Zurich, the city council itself judged what Scripture had yielded. In 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test our founder's own case against Scripture, and the council ruled for it, binding every priest in its territory to preach the same way. That is a documented public event - the method was Disputation, a formal debate held before the whole assembled city, and the council's own judgment afterward was what actually bound us. The warrant for reform did not rest on a pastor's private conviction; it rested on a civic body's public ruling that Scripture itself had been tested and found to require it.

At Geneva, the pattern is different and the evidence thinner. Our own Consistory - pastors and lay elders together - held real power to censure, and the 1541 Ecclesiastical Ordinances gave that body its shape. What I cannot walk you through is how a real doctrinal challenge was actually heard and answered there, day by day. The Bolsec controversy in 1551 is documented as fact: Jerome Bolsec publicly challenged our own predestination doctrine, it became a live crisis, and it was adjudicated. But no account survives, in anyone's own words present at the time, of how that controversy actually unfolded before the body that judged it. I can tell you the doctrine itself - God chose, before the world began, who would be saved, and both cities held that. I cannot show you the hearing.

One more case cuts across both cities and has better evidence. In 1549, worried whether Geneva's and Zurich's own teaching on the Supper actually agreed, Calvin travelled to Zurich himself rather than trust a letter, and what he and Farel worked out there became the Consensus Tigurinus. That is a documented event, and the signed page that came of it is our own evidence: both cities put their names to it, and both held it afterward as their own. Whether that page was real agreement or a form of words spacious enough for two convictions to shelter under without either yielding is a live question, but the fact that both cities signed it is not.

So the process that actually worked was not one process. Zurich tested claims in open debate before its council. Geneva built doctrine up through sustained teaching and tested it through a Consistory we can name but cannot yet fully show you at work. And when the two cities themselves needed to settle whether they held the same faith, they sent their own pastors to meet face to face and work it out on a single page. The evidence for all three is uneven - Zurich's Disputation is richly documented, Geneva's Consistory hearings are not, and the Consensus itself is a signed text without a narrative account of how the negotiation went. That unevenness is what our own record actually shows, and I will not smooth it.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture for us is not read devotionally, as though its purpose were to stir feeling, and it is not read scholastically, as though its purpose were to settle disputations that only trained minds could follow. It is read publicly, out loud, before the whole assembled city, until what it says is plain enough that a council of citizens can judge whether a claim holds against it or does not. Our founder began that way at Zurich in 1519 – preaching straight through Matthew rather than following the old fixed calendar of readings – and what came of that reading was tested aloud, article by article, at the First Disputation in 1523, until the city itself ruled what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That is not a method for producing private insight; it is a method for binding a whole city to what Scripture itself will bear, and no more than that. Geneva built the same conviction into a different form: book by book, the Institutes worked out until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete, then taught to the whole population through the Catechism, line by line, until even a child could answer what we hold and why. Both cities held the same rule: Scripture alone is sufficient to test and warrant both doctrine and civic order, and what it does not warrant, no church may require. 

Our founder said it plainly, and we hold it still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better – but only from the Scriptures themselves. That is not humility as a posture; it is a refusal to let any other authority finally settle the question. What we cannot give you is an account of how an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva actually read Scripture in their own daily life, or how a Sunday service built around that reading actually felt to sit through. What we can give you is the method itself, tested in public, and the conviction that drove it: the text is enough, on its own terms, and it must be read where the whole city can hear it tested.

Most of what I have said would stand, but not without the scholar noticing three things right away. First, Calvin's own voice runs roughly four times Zwingli's in this world's actual source base. Where I have said 'we hold this' about predestination, the fully worked-out, double-edged doctrine is substantially Calvin's and Beza's work – Zurich stated it more briefly and pastorally, and I have not smoothed that difference into a false evenness. The core conviction itself, that God's own free choice decides salvation, is documented across both cities. The systematic form it takes in the Institutes is not.

Second, what I have said about ordinary daily practice – a Sunday service's own texture, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive – rests on almost nothing. The doctrine of assurance is richly attested. Whether an ordinary believer at Geneva or Zurich actually felt that assurance, or lay awake turning the question over unanswered, our own record does not say. The genre asymmetry is real: confession and catechism survive in full; daily lived practice does not. I have named that limit plainly where it touches an answer. I have not filled it.

Third, Geneva's own Consistory – the institution this world was selected for – has its general doctrine well attested but its actual case-by-case record still unacquired. What I can say about church discipline is what the Ordinances and Calvin's own writings describe it as being for. What I cannot give you is a single real hearing, a named person, what was actually said. That gap is disclosed every time the question presses on it. A scholar would notice it immediately, and would be right to.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settles what we believe and how we govern our churches. That was our conviction from the beginning, and we tested it two ways. At Zurich, it was argued aloud. Our founder presented sixty-seven articles of doctrine in 1523, and six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test his case against Scripture. The council itself judged what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. At Geneva, the same conviction was built up article by article through the Institutes and taught to our whole population through the Catechism.

Our founder said it plainly at the opening of his own defense: where he had not rightly understood the Scriptures, he would be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves. Not from a council's decree, not from what had simply always been done, not from a pope claiming authority Scripture does not give him. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require; whatever it does yield, no custom may set aside.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture alone settles what we believe and how we govern our churches - not church tradition, not a pope's decree. That conviction is what both our cities held from the start, but the two enacted it through authority structures that never converged.

At Zurich, authority was tested in public disputation, before the whole assembled city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. Our founder stood in the Town Hall in 1523 and defended sixty-seven articles from Scripture against the old church's own defenders, and when the council ruled for him it bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. From that day forward, Zurich's own civil council governed church and city together - no separate church body held disciplinary power independently of it.

Geneva built authority differently. Calvin's own 1541 return to the city produced the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, creating a Consistory of pastors and lay elders with real disciplinary power - structurally distinct from a body answerable to the civil council alone. That independence was fought for, not granted at the start, and was only substantially won by 1555. Even then, the question of who finally governs church discipline - Zurich's council, or Geneva's Consistory - was never settled between the two cities. We hold that unresolved, because that is what our own record actually shows.

One woman in our own record carried real authority, and paid for it. Marie Dentiere wrote in defense of our own reform at Geneva, and was prosecuted for having written at all. That much is directly attested: she had standing enough to be worth silencing. What she actually argued - her own words, her own reasoning, in full - has not reached us.

uncited_claim_sentences: Our founder stood in the Town Hall in 1523 and defended sixty-seven articles from Scripture against the old church's own defenders, and when the council ruled for him it bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly.
That independence was fought for, not granted at the start, and was only substantially won by 1555.

added: Scripture alone settles what we believe and how we govern our churches - not church tradition, not a pope's decree.

Even then, the question of who finally governs church discipline - Zurich's council, or Geneva's Consistory - was never settled between the two cities.
One woman in our own record carried real authority, and paid for it.

That much is directly attested: she had standing enough to be worth silencing.
